The pure class interface. 
public class BufferSeq<A>
  extends Seq<A>
Implementation variant of sequences which is optimzed for appending and prepending.

This variant of sequences provides in average constant costs for appending or prepending. It is nearly as fast as array sequences according to access functions, but not as compact since it allocates element storage in advance.

The implementation of this sequence variant exploits single threadedness w.r.t. to appending and prepending, such that in a consecutive sequence of operations 

   buf = buf.append(x1);
   buf = buf.prepend(x2);
   buf = buf.append(x3);
   ...
no copies of the contents of the aggregate are necessary for the intermediate values; thus the complexity is in average O(1).

Technically, buffers are represented as arrays with a lower and an upper fillmark. Several buffers may share the same array, but only one buffer can be the owner. Ownership is inherited to the created buffer of append and prepend operations. For these operations, if the array is owned and is large enough, the new elements are destructively updated. (This implementation technique has been e.g. used for implementing mbuf's in TCP/IP implementations of BSD systems.)

BufferSeq
public BufferSeq(int frontCapacity,
                 int backCapacity,
                 int capacityIncrement);
Construct an empty buffer with the specified front and back initial capacities and capacity increment. The overall initial capacity of the buffer is frontCapacity+backCapacity. The buffer needs to grow after frontCapacity elements have been prepended, and after backCapacity elements have been appended. If you plan to add elements only to the one or the other end, use an initial capacity of zero at the opposite end. Negative values for capacity increment are interpreted as percentage of the current buffer size (hence -100 will double the capacity with each reallocation).

public BufferSeq();

BufferSeq

public BufferSeq(Aggregate<A> other);
Construct a buffer which contains the enumerated elements of another aggregate. This constructor is optimized according to the actual representation of the other aggregate. For example, if the other aggregate is a buffer again, the new buffer simply inherits its internal representation.
